title: The pressor keeps climbing
objective: Recognize adrenal crisis -- hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia -- including after abrupt steroid withdrawal, and give IV fluids and hydrocortisone without delay

brief.situation: 02:00 in a surgical ICU. You are Mrs. Haddad's nurse. She is 67, on day 2 after a bowel resection for an obstruction, transferred from the ward at midnight for low blood pressure. The ordered norepinephrine has gone up twice since midnight.
handover: Two fluid boluses given on the ward. Lactate normal. She is drowsy and says her stomach hurts 'all over'.
Her home medicines include a long-term daily prednisone for rheumatoid arthritis. She has been nothing by mouth since the operation.
Unit protocols: a point-of-care glucose under 70 mg/dL is treated with the protocol's IV dextrose and rechecked; the intensivist is in the unit.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Why is her pressure not responding, and what does she need now?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Adrenal crisis: long-term glucocorticoid stopped abruptly at surgery, plus surgical stress; shock refractory to fluids and vasopressors with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, abdominal pain and drowsiness.
parts.modelAnswer: She's on years of daily prednisone and hasn't had any since surgery. Shock that won't respond to fluid and norepinephrine, with low sodium, high potassium, low glucose and diffuse belly pain, is adrenal crisis until proved otherwise.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Treats the glucose per protocol; tells the intensivist now; IV hydrocortisone immediately (labs drawn first only if it causes no delay) with isotonic saline; does not wait for a stimulation test; does not just keep raising the pressor.
parts.modelAnswer: Treat the glucose, tell the intensivist now and get IV hydrocortisone in with saline. Draw a cortisol first only if it doesn't slow the steroid down. No waiting for a stimulation test, and more norepinephrine alone won't fix it.

arrest.headline: Refractory shock
arrest.body: Shock that won't respond to fluid and pressor in a patient whose long-term steroid has stopped is adrenal crisis. Hydrocortisone goes in immediately; tests never delay it.

recovering.headline: Crisis treated
recovering.body: You treated the glucose, found the missing prednisone, recognized adrenal crisis and got IV hydrocortisone in within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: She has taken prednisone daily for years and has had none for three days. With the stress of surgery, shock that does not respond to fluids and norepinephrine, with low sodium, high potassium, low glucose, diffuse abdominal pain and drowsiness, is adrenal crisis. Treat the glucose per protocol, tell the intensivist now, and give IV hydrocortisone at once with isotonic saline. A cortisol and ACTH can be drawn first only if that causes no delay; a stimulation test never comes before the steroid, and more vasopressor alone does not fix it.

causeQ.ask: While you assess: what is the most common cause of adrenal crisis?
causeQ.explain: Abrupt cessation of exogenous corticosteroids is the most common cause; illness, surgery and trauma precipitate it.
